lesson.title: Hired on Merit: The Pendleton Act of 1883
lesson.summary: Signed just over a year after Garfield's assassination, the Pendleton Act created the first real federal civil service system in American history, replacing patronage with competitive exams for a growing share of government jobs.
lesson.body:
Congress responded to the public outcry following Garfield's assassination by passing the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, named for its sponsor, Senator George Pendleton of Ohio. President Chester Arthur, who had emerged as an unexpected champion of reform after taking office, signed the act into law on January 16, 1883.

The law created a bipartisan Civil Service Commission to administer competitive written examinations for a designated set of federal positions, meaning hiring and promotion for those jobs would be based on demonstrated ability rather than political connections or campaign contributions. It also banned the common practice of pressuring federal employees to make political contributions in order to keep their jobs, and it protected employees covered by the new system from being fired simply for refusing to participate in partisan political activity.

The act's reach was limited at first, covering only about one tenth of federal positions and leaving the large majority still subject to patronage. But it contained a mechanism that let its coverage grow over time: it allowed the president to move additional jobs into the protected, merit based "classified" service by executive order. Outgoing presidents from both parties, eager to protect their own appointees from the next administration's spoils system, repeatedly expanded this classified list in the following decades, so that by the twentieth century the great majority of federal civilian jobs fell under merit based rules.

The Pendleton Act marked the beginning of a more professional and less corrupt federal government and set a pattern that many state and city governments later followed, even though it did not eliminate patronage from American political life altogether. It remains one of the clearest examples in American history of a single shocking event, the assassination of a president by a disappointed office seeker, translating public outrage into a lasting institutional reform.
